Working with Sleeve Editions

How to make one sleeve name mean different things for different strategic portfolios, what the rules do, and how to tell the tool has understood you.

For whoever maintains the sleeve library Screens captured from a live console, not mocked up Written 13 September 2026

The idea in one minute

A sleeve used to be one thing: a name and a list of products. It is now a name that can hold more than one version of itself, and each version says which strategic portfolios it is for. A PWA still picks the name. The tool works out which version applies to the portfolio they are building and serves that one. They are never asked to choose, and never told which they got.

Name

What a PWA picks in the rail: “SMA Only”. Unchanged, and the only thing they ever see.

Edition

One version behind that name, with its own products, weights and rules. You give it a short label for your own use.

Fallback

The edition with no rules. It applies wherever no other edition of that name does. Everything in the library today is one.

What a rule actually is

A rule is a sentence about a strategic portfolio, made of three parts:

PartValuesWhat leaving it blank means
CurrencyUSD, GBP, CHF, EURAny currency
Risk levelLowVol through All Equity, eight of themAny risk level
AllocationFull, Core, ex-Alts, ex-HFs, and NA for the all-equity bookAny allocation

Two things follow from that, and they are the whole of the grammar.

  • Ticking several boxes in one row means “any of these”. Currency GBP and EUR ticked together means a GBP portfolio matches, and so does a EUR one.
  • Ticking boxes in different rows narrows. Currency GBP with Allocation ex-Alts means GBP and ex-Alts. Both have to be true.

When one rule cannot say what you mean, add a second. An edition applies where any of its rules matches, so several rules are alternatives, not extra conditions.

Two things are deliberately not rule fields. Currency hedging, and the real-assets exclusion. A rule about GBP Full covers both the plain book and its ex-RAs variant, and a rule never distinguishes Hedged from Unhedged. If you find yourself needing either, that is a change to discuss rather than something to work around.

The walkthrough

We will take the delivered “SMA Only” sleeve in Investment Grade Fixed Income and give it three editions: one for most GBP portfolios, one for GBP ex-Alts, and one shared by EUR and CHF at Moderate. Every screen below is the real console.

Open the repository and find the sleeve

The console icons sit at the foot of the rail. Pick the implementation type along the top, the category on the left, then the sleeve.

Look at the Edition field

Every existing sleeve is a fallback: the field is empty, there are no rules, and the line underneath says so. Leave it alone and nothing about that sleeve changes.

Add an edition and label it

Add edition in the footer starts a new edition of the same name, pre-filled with the products of the one you had open, so you edit rather than retype. The name is locked: editions share it. Type a short label — it is for you and the record, never for a PWA.

Add a rule

An empty rule constrains nothing, so the tool will not save it. Tick what you mean.

Tick, and read the count

Tick GBP and the line underneath answers straight away: 43 of 172 strategic portfolios. That number is the point of the whole screen. It is not an estimate; the tool has expanded your rule against every portfolio the database delivered and counted them.

Save, and see it grouped

The name now shows as a group with its editions underneath: the fallback, and the GBP edition with the portfolios it claims. A name with a single fallback still looks exactly as it always did.

Add a second edition, and meet the refusal

Now a GBP ex-Alts edition. Tick GBP and ex-Alts, and the line turns red: those 7 portfolios are already claimed by the GBP edition, which takes all 43. Save stays disabled.

This is the rule that keeps the whole thing predictable: exactly one edition may apply to a portfolio. If two could, the tool would have to pick, and nobody reading the library could say which.

Fix it by narrowing the broad one

Go back to the GBP edition and say which allocations it is for: Full, Core, ex-HFs and NA, but not ex-Alts. The count drops to 36. Thirty-six plus seven is the same forty-three, now with nothing claimed twice.

Narrow the broad edition, not the specific one. The specific one is the exception you actually wanted; the broad one is the thing that needs to make room for it.

Two rules, when one will not do

For an edition shared by EUR Moderate and CHF Moderate, one rule cannot say it: ticking both currencies and Moderate would be right here, but the moment the two halves differ — say EUR Moderate together with GBP Full — you need two rules. Add another rule and the second is an alternative, marked or.

The finished sleeve

One name, four editions, every portfolio accounted for exactly once.

How the tool picks

Given the portfolio a PWA is building, for each sleeve name:

  1. Does an edition's rules match it? Serve that edition.
  2. Otherwise, is there a fallback? Serve the fallback.
  3. Otherwise the name is not offered at all for that portfolio. That is a legitimate state, not an error: it is how you say “this sleeve is for sterling only”.

Here is that actually happening, read back from the library we just built:

The PWA's base portfolioGetsWhy
GBP | Moderate | ex-AltsGBP ex-AltsThe narrow rule matches
GBP | Moderate | FullGBPGBP, and Full is one of its allocations
GBP | Agg | CoreGBPRisk level is blank in that rule, so any
EUR | Moderate | FullEUR / CHF ModerateRule 1 matches
CHF | Moderate | CoreEUR / CHF ModerateRule 2 matches
EUR | Agg | FullFallbackEUR, but not Moderate
USD | Moderate | FullFallbackNothing names USD

What the PWA sees

Nothing. That is the design, and it is worth seeing. This is the rail on a GBP Moderate ex-Alts mandate, which is being served the GBP ex-Alts edition:

One entry, called “SMA Only”, exactly as before. No label, no badge, no hint that editions exist. The workbook says nothing about it either. A PWA picks a sleeve by name and gets the right products for their portfolio, which is the entire promise.

One consequence to know about. If a PWA changes the base portfolio after choosing sleeves, the tool re-checks every choice against the new portfolio. A name with no edition for it is dropped, and the rail says which and why. There is never a silent substitution.

Managing them

Label them for the person reading the list, not for the machine

The label is free text and it never leaves the console, the history and the exports. “GBP ex-Alts” is a good label. “v2” is not, because in six months the list will show four editions and no way to tell them apart.

Three shapes that cover most of what you will want

What you wantHow
One version everywhere, another for sterlingKeep the fallback. Add one edition, one rule, currency GBP.
A general sterling version, plus an exceptionTwo editions. Give the broad one every allocation except the exception's, so they do not overlap.
Two unrelated groups sharing one versionOne edition, two rules.

Check the arithmetic, not your intention

The count is the check. If you meant “all of sterling” and it says 36 rather than 43, seven portfolios are somewhere else, which is either what you wanted or a sign you have forgotten an edition. The list shows every edition's count side by side for exactly this.

Everything is on the record

An edition is a sleeve as far as the history is concerned: its own revisions, its own put this version back, its own archive entry. Changing a label or a rule is a revision like changing a weight, and the history says which. A proposal already exported is pinned to the edition and revision it was built from, so it never moves under you.

Delivering editions by spreadsheet

The same thing can arrive as data instead of being typed. Two sheets in ProposalTool_DataTemplates.xlsx:

SheetWhat goes in it
sleevesThe products, as before, plus an Edition column. Blank means the fallback. Weights sum to 1 per edition.
sleeveRulesOne row per rule: Variant, Category, Sleeve, Edition, then Currency, RiskLevel, AllocationType. A blank cell means any; several values in a cell are separated by a vertical bar, as in Full|Core|ex-HFs|NA. Two rows for the same edition are two alternatives.

The three editions built above would be delivered like this:

SleeveEditionCurrencyRiskLevelAllocationType
SMA OnlyGBPGBPFull|Core|ex-HFs|NA
SMA OnlyGBP ex-AltsGBPex-Alts
SMA OnlyEUR / CHF ModerateEURModerate
SMA OnlyEUR / CHF ModerateCHFModerate

The last two rows are one edition with two rules. A delivery is checked exactly as a save is, and a bad one is refused whole with the reason named, so nothing half-loads.

What gets refused, and why

If you try toYou are toldBecause
Save two editions of one name claiming the same portfolioWhich portfolios clash, by nameExactly one edition may apply, or the answer is unpredictable
Give an edition rules but no labelGive the edition a labelThe list and the history would have nothing to call it
Give it a label but no rulesAdd a rule, or clear the labelA labelled edition that applies everywhere is a second fallback in disguise
Add a second fallbackThat name already exists hereThe same clash it always was, now stated in terms of editions
Add a rule with nothing tickedEvery rule needs a valueAn unconstrained rule claims everything
Name a currency or level the database does not haveWhich value, and what is knownAlmost always a typo, and it would silently match nothing

One case you may meet later. If the strategic universe changes under two editions that were fine when saved, they can end up claiming the same portfolio after the fact. The tool does not pick one: it withholds that name for the affected portfolio and flags both editions as broken in the console, the same way it flags a sleeve whose product has left the catalogue. Narrow one of them and it clears.

Quick reference

Blank field in a rule
Any value. Not “none”.
Several ticks in one row
Any of these.
Ticks in different rows
All of these, together.
Several rules
Alternatives. The edition applies where any one matches.
Empty label, no rules
The fallback. Applies where nothing else does.
Label with rules
A scoped edition. Applies only where its rules say.
The green line
How many of the 172 strategic portfolios this claims.
The red line
Which portfolios another edition already claims. Save is blocked.
A name with no fallback
Offered only where one of its editions applies.
What the PWA sees
The name. Never the edition.
